data.title: Kinki Sharyo's (TSE:7122) Solid Earnings Are Supported By Other Strong Factors
data.description:
The Kinki Sharyo Co., Ltd. (TSE:7122) announced strong profits, but the stock was stagnant. Our analysis suggests that shareholders have noticed something concerning in the numbers.

This technology could replace computers: discover the 20 stocks are working to make quantum computing a reality.

Zooming In On Kinki Sharyo's Earnings

Many investors haven't heard of the accrual ratio from cashflow, but it is actually a useful measure of how well a company's profit is backed up by free cash flow (FCF) during a given period. To get the accrual ratio we first subtract FCF from profit for a period, and then divide that number by the average operating assets for the period. You could think of the accrual ratio from cashflow as the 'non-FCF profit ratio'.

That means a negative accrual ratio is a good thing, because it shows that the company is bringing in more free cash flow than its profit would suggest. While having an accrual ratio above zero is of little concern, we do think it's worth noting when a company has a relatively high accrual ratio. Notably, there is some academic evidence that suggests that a high accrual ratio is a bad sign for near-term profits, generally speaking.

Kinki Sharyo has an accrual ratio of -0.24 for the year to September 2026. That indicates that its free cash flow quite significantly exceeded its statutory profit. In fact, it had free cash flow of JP¥8.5b in the last year, which was a lot more than its statutory profit of JP¥1.40b. Given that Kinki Sharyo had negative free cash flow in the prior corresponding period, the trailing twelve month resul of JP¥8.5b would seem to be a step in the right direction. However, that's not all there is to consider. The accrual ratio is reflecting the impact of unusual items on statutory profit, at least in part.

How Do Unusual Items Influence Profit?

While the accrual ratio might bode well, we also note that Kinki Sharyo's profit was boosted by unusual items worth JP¥878m in the last twelve months. While we like to see profit increases, we tend to be a little more cautious when unusual items have made a big contribution. When we crunched the numbers on thousands of publicly listed companies, we found that a boost from unusual items in a given year is often not repeated the next year. Which is hardly surprising, given the name. We can see that Kinki Sharyo's positive unusual items were quite significant relative to its profit in the year to September 2026. As a result, we can surmise that the unusual items are making its statutory profit significantly stronger than it would otherwise be.

Our Take On Kinki Sharyo's Profit Performance

In conclusion, Kinki Sharyo's accrual ratio suggests its statutory earnings are of good quality, but on the other hand the profits were boosted by unusual items. Given the contrasting considerations, we don't have a strong view as to whether Kinki Sharyo's profits are an apt reflection of its underlying potential for profit. The Two StoneCo Stories Investors Had To Weigh

The bullish case, with a Fair Value of US$17.64 treated as the price implied by its assumptions, leaned on divesting software assets and using that cash for higher margin financial services and share buybacks.

A Closer Look At Superbag Company's Earnings

Many investors haven't heard of the accrual ratio from cashflow, but it is actually a useful measure of how well a company's profit is backed up by free cash flow (FCF) during a given period. In plain english, this ratio subtracts FCF from net profit, and divides that number by the company's average operating assets over that period. This ratio tells us how much of a company's profit is not backed by free cashflow.

Therefore, it's actually considered a good thing when a company has a negative accrual ratio, but a bad thing if its accrual ratio is positive. While having an accrual ratio above zero is of little concern, we do think it's worth noting when a company has a relatively high accrual ratio. Notably, there is some academic evidence that suggests that a high accrual ratio is a bad sign for near-term profits, generally speaking.

For the year to September 2026, Superbag Company had an accrual ratio of 0.44. Statistically speaking, that's a real negative for future earnings. And indeed, during the period the company didn't produce any free cash flow whatsoever. Even though it reported a profit of JP¥663.0m, a look at free cash flow indicates it actually burnt through JP¥2.1b in the last year. It's worth noting that Superbag Company generated positive FCF of JP¥626m a year ago, so at least they've done it in the past. Having said that, there is more to the story. The accrual ratio is reflecting the impact of unusual items on statutory profit, at least in part.

The Impact Of Unusual Items On Profit

While we like to see profit increases, we tend to be a little more cautious when unusual items have made a big contribution. When we analysed the vast majority of listed companies worldwide, we found that significant unusual items are often not repeated. Which is hardly surprising, given the name. Superbag Company had a rather significant contribution from unusual items relative to its profit to September 2026. data.description:
There's no doubt that money can be made by owning shares of unprofitable businesses. Having said that, unprofitable companies are risky because they could potentially burn through all their cash and become distressed.

When Might VELTRA Run Out Of Money?

A company's cash runway is calculated by dividing its cash hoard by its cash burn. When VELTRA last reported its June 2026 balance sheet in August 2026, it had zero debt and cash worth JP¥4.9b. In the last year, its cash burn was JP¥788m. So it had a cash runway of about 6.3 years from June 2026. Is VELTRA's Revenue Growing?

How Hard Would It Be For VELTRA To Raise More Cash For Growth?

Since its revenue growth is moving in the wrong direction, VELTRA shareholders may wish to think ahead to when the company may need to raise more cash. Generally speaking, a listed business can raise new cash through issuing shares or taking on debt. Commonly, a business will sell new shares in itself to raise cash and drive growth. By comparing a company's annual cash burn to its total market capitalisation, we can estimate roughly how many shares it would have to issue in order to run the company for another year (at the same burn rate).

VELTRA's cash burn of JP¥788m is about 18% of its JP¥4.3b market capitalisation. As a result, we'd venture that the company could raise more cash for growth without much trouble, albeit at the cost of some dilution.

The lesson is simple. When a thesis hangs on demand for a specific product set, like Prysmian’s high tech grid and fiber cables, track signed multi year agreements, committed capex and contracted project work rather than headline price targets.

data.title: How £7b Loan Risk Sale Will Impact NatWest Shares (LSE:NWG)
data.description:
• NatWest Group has received regulatory approval for its Targeted Support service and completed a significant risk transfer on about £7b of large corporate loans. This adjusts how it manages customer guidance and credit exposure.
  • The combination of targeted investment support for retail clients and first loss risk transfer on corporate loans reshapes how NatWest balances fee potential, balance sheet usage and protection for both customers and shareholders.
  • We will look at how NatWest's investment narrative is influenced by the £7b corporate loan risk transfer and customer Targeted Support.

Scan how NatWest Group's mix of capital raising, credit risk transfer and retail investment support compares with a hand-picked list of solid balance sheet and fundamentals (7 results).

NatWest Group Investment Narrative Recap

To own NatWest Group, you need to be comfortable with a UK focused bank that leans on interest income today while pushing hard into fee based wealth and payments. The analyst consensus narrative on Simply Wall St frames the key belief as disciplined cost control, AI driven efficiency and steady profit growth rather than rapid expansion. The recent Targeted Support approval and £7b corporate loan risk transfer nudge the story toward advice led retail fees and tighter credit risk management, without clearly changing the near term focus on margins and cost to income.

The most important short term swing factor still sits in net interest margin, which management guides to flatten as lower spread mortgages and Commercial & Institutional loans grow. The biggest operational risk is the mix of rising wholesale funding needs, a loan to deposit ratio around 92% and ongoing UK bank tax uncertainty. The new services and risk transfer support balance sheet resilience and fee potential, but do not remove those pressures.

The Targeted Support approval looks most relevant for your thesis because it links directly to NatWest Group's push into advice and investment services after the Evelyn Partners deal more than doubled assets under management to £131b. Management is targeting a larger share of customer savings and investment flows, which could gradually tilt earnings toward more capital light and recurring fees if execution is solid.

For catalysts and risks, the new support service fits into the same theme as NatWest Group's AI use and Tyl merchant payments work, all aimed at higher value, less balance sheet intensive activities. The key watchpoints now are how quickly Targeted Support is rolled out, how regulators respond to customer outcomes and whether the bank can keep costs in check while fee income grows enough to cushion any pressure on lending spreads.

NatWest Group's narrative projects £20.8 billion revenue and £7.0 billion earnings by 2029. This projection assumes revenue grows at 7.1% per year and earnings rise by about £1.0 billion from £6.0 billion today.
